title: Sixteen, and Lying Still
hookLine: a sixteen-year-old lies down as if dead and asks who dies
carry: atman isn't the body: dive for its source
tomorrow: his friends weep that he's leaving. 'where could I go?' he asks. what did he mean?

lines: HE LIES DOWN AS IF DEAD.
THE BODY IS DEAD. AM I?
cards: Madurai, 1896. A sixteen-year-old schoolboy is sitting alone upstairs in his uncle's house, perfectly healthy, when a sudden, total fear of death comes over him. He doesn't call anyone.
He decides to look at it. He lies down flat and stretches his arms and legs out stiff, the way a body is laid out. He holds his breath and presses his lips shut, so not even the word I can come out.
And he asks: now this body is dead. Am I?

teach.b: In his own later account, the boy, Ramana, reasoned it through. This body will be carried to the burning ground and turned to ash. But is the body I?
Lying there, silent and still, he felt the I fully, apart from the body, untouched by its death. The fear never came back. About six weeks later he left home for Arunachala.
Here's the teaching, one of Hinduism's biggest. The self, atman, isn't the body.

The Gita says it isn't born and doesn't die, and isn't killed when the body is killed. Ramana didn't read that and agree; he went looking. Decades later his Forty Verses describe the same move with a picture.
In paraphrase: as someone dives for a thing fallen into a deep well, dive within, with a keen mind, holding back speech and breath, and find where the I rises. Saying I with the mouth isn't it.
Thinking I am not this, I am That, can help, but it isn't the dive. Later he asks: does a man keep thinking, I am a man? We are That already.
The Sanskrit for I is aham, and these verses hunt for its source instead of adding labels.
Name, age, school, worries: those float on the surface.

teach.h: DIVE FOR WHERE THE I RISES.
teach.b: The dive goes under them, to where the first thought, I, comes up. His followers call this way atma-vichara, self-inquiry. A scared boy upstairs in Madurai did it first.

how: Ramana's way is called self-inquiry, atma-vichara: followers sit quietly and trace the feeling of 'I' back to its source, asking 'who am I?'

o: a Tamil work song sung while drawing water from wells
a Tamil poem that sends you diving for where the I rises
a book of rules for bathing in temple tanks at dawn

p: the boy lies down as if dead

s: Ramana found self-inquiry after years of reading Vedanta books
at sixteen he hadn't; the fear of death came and he looked straight at it.
his verse compares the inquiry to diving into a deep well
holding back speech and breath, with a keen mind.
Ramana's practice is repeating 'I am Brahman' over and over
he calls that a help; the inquiry is seeking where the I rises.

games.q: a friend writes 'i am calm' on a sticky note and reads it over and over. what would Ramana's verses say?
o: a line can help, but the dive is finding where the I rises.
keep reading it; repeating it is the whole path.
throw the note away; words are always useless.
games.why: 'I am That' is a help, the verses say, but the inquiry is turning within to where the I springs up.

practice: Let the mouth go still and the breath slow and easy; there's no need to hold it. Close your eyes and feel the plain sense of being here. Instead of naming it, follow it down, the way a diver follows a glint.
When a thought pulls you up, take an easy breath and go down again.

wordCard.voice: Ramana's Forty Verses: a poem that says the self isn't found by repeating its name, but by diving to where the I rises.

orig.note: Sanskrit: I; the verses hunt for where it rises.

carryVoice: Keep this one: atman isn't the body; dive for its source. A boy of sixteen lay still and found it.

sources.ref: Ramana's account of his death experience, Madurai, July 1896 (lay as a corpse, held breath and closed lips; the body dies, but am I dead? felt the I apart from the body; the fear of death never returned; left for Tiruvannamalai about six weeks later)
sources.work: Arthur Osborne, Ramana Maharshi and the Path of Self-Knowledge (paraphrased)
